918.title: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
918.hook: freed from a slave ship as a boy, he becomes the first African Anglican bishop (1864)
918.howItsDone: Anglicans in Nigeria and beyond remember Crowther in their calendars and prayers, and Yoruba-speaking Christians still read and sing from the Bible and hymns in their own language.

segments.voice: Yesterday, missions and empire, told honestly: schools and hospitals, pride and borrowed power, and local Christians who led, like Ramabai. Your line was the gospel is not an empire. Did you learn a local leader's name? Day nine hundred eighteen.

A Yoruba boy named Ajayi is taken in a raid on his town, in what is now Nigeria. He is sold, and sold again, and finally put in chains on a slave ship bound across the Atlantic. Then, before the ship gets far, a British navy ship stops it. The captives are taken off and brought to Sierra Leone, and set free. The boy who walks off that deck has lost his home, and has no word of his family. He has nothing. Years later, that same boy will walk into a cathedral in England and come out a bishop. Yesterday was the honest story of missions. Today, one of the local Christians who led it: Samuel Ajayi Crowther.
screen: `A YORUBA BOY, TAKEN IN A RAID.`

segments.voice: In Sierra Leone the boy went to a mission school, learned to read quickly, and was baptized, taking the name Samuel Crowther. He kept Ajayi too. He studied, taught, and was ordained a priest. Then he became the thing the missions badly needed: a translator. He worked on putting the Bible into Yoruba, his own first language, and helped with grammars and word lists for other languages along the Niger River. He wanted people to hear the gospel in the words their mothers used. Tradition says that on one trip home, he found his own mother, years after the raid, and that she too was later baptized. Then he was made a bishop, to lead the church's mission on the Niger, and Anglicans remember him as their first African bishop. That's the high point. The story doesn't end clean. In his old age, younger European missionaries criticized his work and pushed his African clergy aside, and he was sidelined. Some who tell his story see in it the same arrogance named yesterday. Hold all of it. Here's the thread through his life. Jesus, reading in the synagogue at Nazareth, chose these words from Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives." Crowther had been a captive. He was delivered. And he spent his life carrying the word that freed him back toward his own people. Paul wrote: "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free." For Crowther, being freed wasn't the end of the story. It was a job.

Here's the practice: pray for Nigeria, or simply hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a country you may know only from headlines. Its cities, its markets, its churches and mosques, its children walking to school this morning. Picture a Yoruba hymn being sung somewhere right now, in a language Crowther helped put on paper. If you pray, you can pray for Nigeria's people, for peace and for daily bread. If you don't, let your attention rest there kindly, one place at a time. The bell holds the time.
Crowther. Freed from a slave ship as a boy, he became a translator of the Bible into Yoruba and the first African Anglican bishop on the Niger.
Your line: freed to free. Today, take one thing someone once did to set you free, and do it for somebody else. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: Sojourner Truth
919.hook: a freed woman preacher who spoke for abolition and women's rights
919.howItsDone: Some churches remember Sojourner Truth as a preacher and reformer, and her story is told in sermons and classes on faith, freedom and women's voices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samuel Ajayi Crowther, freed from a slave ship, then a translator and a bishop. Your line was freed to free. Whose freedom did you help along? Day nine hundred nineteen.

A courtroom in New York. A tall Black woman, once enslaved, stands before the judge. Her young son has been sold away, illegally, to a planter in the South, and she wants him back. Nobody expects her to win. She can't read. She has no money. Her first language isn't even English. She speaks anyway, and she keeps speaking, and she gets her son back. Her name then was Isabella. Later she gave herself a new one, a name that sounds like a job description. A sojourner is someone who travels and doesn't settle. And truth was what she meant to carry. Today: Sojourner Truth.

Isabella was born into slavery in New York, in a household where she grew up speaking Dutch. When freedom was slow in coming, she walked away from her enslaver with her baby daughter in her arms. Not ran, she said later. Walked. Around then her faith became fierce and personal. In the account of her life she dictated, she describes a moment of overwhelming awareness of God, and then of Jesus standing between her and God, a friend. Years later, she said the Spirit was calling her to go out and travel, and so she took the name Sojourner Truth and went: preaching at camp meetings, singing, speaking against slavery, and then, just as boldly, for the rights of women. One speech of hers, given at a women's rights meeting in Ohio, is still quoted today. Here's the honest part: she didn't write it down. Others did, and the versions differ a lot. The famous refrain people quote comes from one later version. But one thread runs through the reports. Men had argued against women's rights from the Bible. She answered from the Bible too, and in at least one version she asks where Christ came from, and answers: from God and a woman. She knew her scripture, and she claimed it. And scripture had room for her. The prophet Joel had said, in the King James Bible: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Daughters too. Paul wrote, "there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Some women preachers of her day pointed to lines like these. She stood up in rooms where nobody wanted to hear a woman, a Black woman, a formerly enslaved woman, say anything at all. She said it anyway.

Here's the practice: get ready to speak up at a meeting. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next room where you'll be asked for your view, or not asked: a work call, a family dinner, a church or school meeting. Notice the thing you've been holding back, the true sentence you keep swallowing. Say it once, silently, plainly, the way you'd want to say it. Then breathe again and picture yourself saying it out loud, calmly, without apology. If you pray, you can ask for courage. If you don't, simply hold the sentence steady. The bell holds the time.
Sojourner Truth. A name she chose: a traveler, carrying truth, who preached against slavery and for the rights of women.
Your line: a woman speaks. Today, in one meeting or conversation, say the true sentence you've been holding back, or make room for someone else to say theirs. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Harriet Tubman
920.hook: she escaped slavery and went back, again and again, guided by prayer
920.howItsDone: Some churches tell Tubman's story in services on freedom and justice, and spirituals like Go Down, Moses are still sung in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sojourner Truth, who walked away from slavery and then answered the Bible with the Bible. Your line was a woman speaks. Did you say the sentence you'd been holding back? Day nine hundred twenty.

She has made it. After nights of walking, hiding in woods and following the North Star, she crosses into a free state. She said later that she looked at her hands to see if she was the same person. There was such a glory over everything, she said, she felt like she was in heaven. And then the thought arrives. Her family is still back there. Her brothers, her parents, her friends. She is free, and she is alone. Plenty of stories would end at the border. This one turns around and walks back toward the danger. Today: Harriet Tubman.

Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland. As a girl, she was struck in the head by a heavy weight an overseer threw at someone else, and for the rest of her life she had spells and vivid dreams that she understood as God speaking to her. After her escape, she went back into slave country again and again, bringing out family members and others, traveling by night along what people called the Underground Railroad. She was remembered as saying she never lost a passenger. The thing to hear today is how she did it. She prayed, constantly, plainly, the way you'd talk to a friend. The people who knew her said she spoke with God as someone she trusted completely, and that she moved when she felt led and waited when she felt warned. And people gave her a name from scripture: Moses. In the book of Exodus, God says to Moses, in the King James Bible: "Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt." And Moses carries a message to Pharaoh: "Let my people go." Enslaved people sang about that very story. Tradition says Tubman used songs like Go Down, Moses as signals, to tell people she was near. Why does that name land so hard? Because Moses didn't only escape. Moses had already gotten out of Egypt, and was sent back. That's Tubman exactly. The freedom she found was never meant to stay hers alone.

Here's the practice: go back for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you've gotten out of: a hard season, a bad job, a habit, a grief, a lonely stretch. Now think of someone who is still in it. Let their face come clearly. Don't plan a rescue yet. Just turn around in your mind and look back toward them, the way she turned at the border. Ask what one small thing would help them find the way. If you pray, you can ask to be led, the way she asked. If you don't, keep looking back with kindness. The bell holds the time.
Harriet Tubman. She escaped slavery, went back for others again and again, and prayed the whole way. People called her Moses.
Your line: the moses of her people. Today, reach back to one person still in a place you've left, with a call, a message or a door held open. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: Douglass on two Christianities
921.hook: Frederick Douglass rejected slaveholders' religion and loved the Christianity of Christ
921.howItsDone: Some Christians read Douglass's appendix in churches, classes and seminaries as a test of their own faith, sometimes alongside the prophets and the letter of James.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Harriet Tubman, who reached freedom and turned around to go back. Your line was the moses of her people. Who did you reach back for? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

The last page is written. It's the story of a life in slavery, told by the man who lived it, and it's sharp, and angry, and full of church people: an enslaver who got religion at a camp meeting and became crueler afterward, a man who led prayers in his house and used the whip in his fields. The author reads it over and realizes something. A reader might close this book thinking he hates religion altogether. So he sits down again and adds a few more pages at the very end, to make himself clear. Those added pages hold hard words about the church, from a man who loved Christ. Today: Frederick Douglass, on two Christianities.
screen: `A FEW PAGES ADDED AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Douglass had escaped slavery and become a speaker against it. In his Narrative, he tells what he saw: enslavers who were church members, even preachers, and who were no kinder for it. He writes that the religious slaveholders he knew were the worst of all. So at the end of the book he adds an appendix, and says plainly what he meant. Here are his words: "between the Christianity of this land, and the Christianity of Christ, I recognize the widest possible difference." And then: "I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ." Hear the three words he chose, set against the slaveholding religion he describes. Pure: not mixed with profit. Peaceable: not backed by the whip. Impartial: not taking sides by the color of someone's skin. And he says he hates the other kind, the slaveholding religion, with the same force. He wasn't attacking faith from the outside. He was making a distinction from the inside, the way the prophets did. Scripture offers a test of its own. The letter of James says, in the King James Bible: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Set that beside one of the words Douglass used for the slaveholders' religion: "cradle-plundering." A faith that cares for orphans, and a faith that takes children from their mothers, can sing the same hymns on Sunday. For Douglass, they were still not the same faith. The question he leaves is a hard one for any believer, in any century: which Christianity is mine?

Here's the practice: tell apart the real and the fake. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you do in the name of what you believe, or in the name of being a good person. A habit, a cause, a way you treat people. Hold it up against Douglass's three words. Is it pure, or mixed with something you're getting out of it? Is it peaceable, or does it lean on force? Is it impartial, or does it quietly prefer some people over others? Don't punish yourself. Just look honestly. If you pray, you can ask to see clearly. The bell holds the time.
Frederick Douglass. The escaped former slave whose narrative named two Christianities, the slaveholders' religion and the pure, peaceable Christianity of Christ he loved.
Your line: the christianity of christ. Today, when you see faith used to hurt someone, ask Douglass's question: is this pure, peaceable and impartial? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: The invisible church
922.hook: enslaved Christians met in secret hush harbors to pray and sing
922.howItsDone: Spirituals like Steal Away are still sung in Black churches, and some congregations remember the hush harbors in services that honor the faith of enslaved ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frederick Douglass on two Christianities: the slaveholders' religion, and the Christianity of Christ he loved. Your line was the christianity of christ. Where did you see the difference? Day nine hundred twenty-two.

Servants, obey your masters. On a plantation, that is the sermon from the enslaver's preacher, the one formerly enslaved people would later remember hearing. They sit through it. Then night comes. One by one, quietly, people slip out of the cabins and into the woods, down to a hollow or a gully where the trees are thick. Someone has hung wet quilts on branches. Somebody has set an iron pot on the ground, upside down. And there, in the dark, a different church begins. Today: the invisible church.

Historians call it the invisible institution, or the invisible church, and people who lived it called the meeting places hush harbors. Being caught there could mean a beating, so everything was built for silence. In the memories of formerly enslaved people, written down later, the wet quilts and the turned-over pot come up more than once: ways, they believed, to catch and soften the sound. There, the remembered preaching was different. Some of the slaveholders' sermons leaned on one line from Paul, in the King James Bible: "Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters." In the hush harbor, people preached Exodus instead: a God who hears the cry of slaves and brings them out. They preached Jesus, who suffered and rose. They prayed out loud, called out, moaned, sang, and sometimes shouted, all as quietly as they could. And they sang songs we now call spirituals. One of them is the source of today's line: steal away, steal away to Jesus. On the surface, it's a song about going to God. Some people say it was also a call to the next secret meeting, and later a hint about escape. Tradition holds both meanings together, and the song doesn't explain itself. Jesus had said: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." No building. No permission. No preacher hired by the master. Just people gathered in the dark, sure that Christ was there with them. That hidden church is one of the roots of the Black church in America, alongside the churches free Black Christians were already building in the open, like Richard Allen's in Philadelphia.

Here's the practice: pray quietly in a hidden place, or simply sit there. Find somewhere small and out of the way: a closet, a car, a corner, a stairwell, a spot behind a tree. Settle, and breathe. Let your voice drop to nothing. Remember the people who met in the hollows at night, risking everything just to be together and to sing. If you pray, you can pray there in a whisper, or without words at all. If you don't, let the quiet place hold you, and remember them. The bell holds the time.
Hush harbors. The secret meeting places in the woods where enslaved Christians gathered at night to pray, preach and sing their own faith.
Your line: steal away. Today, find one hidden minute, step out of the noise, and be still somewhere out of sight. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: Seraphim in the snow
923.hook: Seraphim of Sarov shows his friend Motovilov the Spirit's light shining in a snowy forest
923.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians honor Seraphim of Sarov as a saint, read Motovilov's account of their conversation, and speak of the aim of the Christian life as acquiring the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hush harbors, praying in the woods at night where no master could hear. Your line was steal away. Did you find your hidden minute? Day nine hundred twenty-three.

Winter in a Russian forest. Snow is falling thickly in a clearing. An old monk in a worn white robe, bent with age and old injuries, sits on a tree stump. Crouched in front of him is a younger man, a landowner, who has come with a question he can't let go of. All his life he's heard that the point of being a Christian is to receive the Holy Spirit. Fine. But how would anyone actually know? What does it look like? The old monk takes him firmly by the shoulders. And then something happens in the snow that the younger man later tries to put into words. Today: Seraphim in the snow.

The monk is Seraphim of Sarov, honored as a saint in the Orthodox Church. The younger man is Nicholas Motovilov, and he wrote the conversation down. Here's how he tells it, paraphrased. Seraphim says the true aim of the Christian life is the acquiring of the Holy Spirit. Prayer, fasting and good works matter, but as means to that. Motovilov keeps asking how he can know. So Seraphim grips his shoulders and says, in effect: we are both in the Spirit now. Why won't you look at me? Motovilov says he can't. Seraphim's face has become brighter than the sun, too bright to look at. And Seraphim answers: don't be afraid. You've become just as bright yourself, or you couldn't see me like this. Then he asks, again and again, what do you feel? And Motovilov answers. A quiet, a peace he has no words for. A sweetness. Joy. And warmth, even though the snow is still falling on them and settling on their coats. Seraphim connects it to Paul, in the King James Bible: "For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." In Motovilov's telling, peace and joy were not a reward for later. They were the Spirit, there, in the cold. A saying handed down in Seraphim's name gives today's line its fuller shape: acquire the spirit of peace, and thousands around you will be saved. In that saying, the change starts small, inside one person, and moves outward like warmth in a cold room.

Here's the practice: stand in snow or cold air, and pray, or simply be still. If you can, open a window or step outside. Feel the cold on your face and hands. Breathe in, and notice how sharp it is. Breathe out, and watch your breath if you can see it. Then let the question Seraphim kept asking land on you: what do you feel, right now? Name it honestly. If you pray, you can ask quietly for the Spirit's peace. If you don't, let the stillness and the cold be enough. The bell holds the time.
Motovilov. The landowner who asked Seraphim of Sarov how to know the Holy Spirit, and said he felt peace, warmth and joy in the falling snow.
Your line: acquire the spirit of peace. Today, before you walk into a tense room, take one slow breath and bring peace in with you, instead of picking up the tension. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

924.title: The Way of a Pilgrim
924.hook: an anonymous Russian wanderer tries to pray without ceasing, using the Jesus Prayer
924.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians, and some Catholics and Protestants, pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a prayer rope, repeating it quietly through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seraphim in the snow, and Motovilov, the friend who felt peace and warmth in a winter forest. Your line was acquire the spirit of peace. Did you carry peace into a tense room? Day nine hundred twenty-four.

Pray without ceasing. The line is read out in church from one of Paul's letters, and a man standing there feels it catch like a hook in cloth. He can't shake it. Without ceasing? How? People have to work, and eat, and sleep. So he leaves, with a knapsack, some dried bread and a Bible, and starts walking, asking preachers and monks how it's done. Nobody gives him an answer that works. A little book tells all this, in his own voice. He never gives his name. He calls himself only a wanderer, a pilgrim. Today: The Way of a Pilgrim.

The line is from Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, in the King James Bible, and it's just three words: "Pray without ceasing." The pilgrim wanders until, the book says, he meets an elder, a starets, who finally answers him. The answer is a very short prayer, said over and over: the Jesus Prayer. Its usual words are Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Its roots are in the Gospels. A blind man by the road at Jericho calls out: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." And a tax collector in one of Jesus's parables stands far off and prays: "God be merciful to me a sinner." The elder sets the pilgrim a task: say the prayer a set number of times each day, using a prayer rope to keep his place, and then more. At first it's work, like learning to walk again. Then, the pilgrim says, something shifts. The prayer starts to say itself. It moves from his lips into his heart, falls into the rhythm of his breath, keeps time with his heartbeat. He walks for miles with it running quietly underneath everything, and the world starts to look different: people kinder, trees and grass full of God. That's the book's answer to pray without ceasing. Not a voice that never stops talking. A prayer that keeps going underneath, like a heartbeat. It closes a week of people whose faith was lived, not only spoken: Crowther, Truth, Tubman, Douglass, the hush harbors, Seraphim. Today it's a wanderer, walking.

Here's the practice: pray one line while walking, or walk with one line. Stand up if you can, and walk slowly: around the room, down a hall, along the block. Let your steps find an easy rhythm. If you pray, you can use the Jesus Prayer, or the blind man's words, have mercy on me, one phrase on each step or each breath. If you don't pray, choose one short true line and let it keep time with your feet. When your mind wanders, come back gently to the line. The bell holds the time.
Jesus Prayer. The short prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner, that the nameless pilgrim learned to say without ceasing.
Your line: pray without ceasing. Today, pick one short line and let it run under one ordinary task: the dishes, the commute, the walk to the car. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

original.note: Greek: without ceasing, unceasingly — the word in 1 Thessalonians 5:17, pray without ceasing.

trapdoor: what you thought: praying all day long means never doing anything else.

what a scholar hears: Paul's three words in 1 Thessalonians 5:17, answered by the Jesus Prayer, rooted in the Gospels' have mercy on me.
